newsitem.title: UK: Shell says expects to lose Saudi oil-for-arms deal.
newsitem.headline: Shell says expects to lose Saudi oil-for-arms deal.

text.p: Royal Dutch/Shell Group said on Thursday it expected at the end of the year to lose the right to market Saudi Arabian crude oil covered by the $2 billion Al-Yamamah oil-for-arms deal.

Under the terms of the decade-old arrangement, Shell and British Petroleum Co Plc market internally some 400,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Saudi crude, passing the proceeds to British Aerospace Plc which in turn supplies Tornado fighter jets to Riyadh.
State-owned Saudi Aramco has said it wants to take control of the sales from January 1 and the oil majors look to have lost a last-minute effort to gain an extension of the contract.
Shell confirmed the existing arrangements were likely to come to an end but said it would continue to take delivery of similar quantities of Saudi crude for its refining system.
"The contract is not expected to be renewed," said Eric Nickson, spokesman for Shell, which takes two-thirds of the crude.
He was unable to provide further information about whether the crude would be supplied on standard commercial terms from the turn of the year.
BP officials were unavailable for comment.

The arms-for-oil swap -- extended in 1992 to cover a further 200,000 bpd marketed directly by Aramco -- will be unaffected by the new arrangements which form part of a broader strategy by Riyadh to gain greater control of its crude exports and generate higher income.

Aramco has taken a half share in the Greek Vardinoyannis oil group, which owns the 100,000 bpd Motor Oil Hellas refinery and is talking to Portuguese state oil company Petrogal about the possibility of setting up a joint venture.
Analysts say Aramco's decision to terminate the marketing deal could prove a double blow to Shell and BP.

Apart from earning substantial commissions of 15-20 cents a barrel on the sales, their global refining operations allow both companies to buy the crude in the cheapest market -- Aramco sets different price formulas for Asian, U.S. and European customers on a monthly basis -- and use the crude where refining margins are most profitable.
Aramco -- which markets about six million bpd -- usually requires customers to declare where the crude is going before it will agree to the nomination.
The loss of the freedom to move crude between markets, taking advantage of arbitrage opportunities, could be the biggest blow, analysts said.
"If they can still buy the crude on the formula of their choice they've still got a money spinner -- the big bucks were made playing the arbitrage," said one industry source.
Trading revenues could suffer by millions of dollars, sources said.
"It will be interesting to see Stasco (Shell International Trading and Shipping Co)'s figures for next year," said one.
